Rain hammered the bus shelter, and the last bus was forty minutes late. Asif sat with his elbows on his knees. He had been cut from the school football squad that afternoon. "I'm done. I'll never make anything of it."
Neelam didn't say it would be fine. She sat down next to him and let the rain fill the quiet. After a while she said, "That's really rough. You practised all term."
He nodded, jaw tight.
"There's another trial in January, isn't there?"
"Yeah."
"We could run drills on Sunday mornings. Ten laps, then see what the coach says."
"You'd do that?"
"I've got nothing on Sundays."
The bus lights appeared down the road, and for a moment neither of them moved.

qa.q: How late was the last bus?
qa.a: The last bus was forty minutes late.

qa.q: How might Neelam have been feeling as she sat in the rain with Asif?
qa.a: Neelam was probably worried and caring, choosing to stay and listen. Her offer of Sundays suggests she wanted to be useful.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that offered hope without empty promises?
qa.a: Neelam stayed beside him without saying it would be fine, acknowledged the effort, and pointed to the January trial with a small plan of Sunday drills.

qa.q: How might Asif have seen Neelam sitting beside him without saying it would be fine?
qa.a: As real support. Asif was crushed after being cut from the squad, with a tight jaw, and Neelam's company and small plan gave him something to hold on to.

grounding: A friend responds to despair by staying, listening and pointing to a small next step, not insisting everything will be fine.

Irawati sat on the school stairs with her chess bag, staring at her shoes. "I blundered in the final. I'm just a bad player."
Rafiq sat one step below. He didn't tell her it was nothing. "That was a hard game. I watched your opening. It was really sharp."
She looked up. "It doesn't matter now."
"It matters. Do you want to look at the game tomorrow at lunch? I'll bring my board."
She thought about it. "Maybe. Not the whole game."
"Just the mistake, then."
She nodded slowly and picked up her bag. At the bottom of the stairs she said, "Thanks for not saying it was fine."
"It wasn't fine," said Rafiq. "But it's not the end."

qa.q: Where did Irawati sit after the final?
qa.a: Irawati sat on the school stairs.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have been feeling as he sat one step below and would not say it was nothing?
qa.a: Rafiq was probably concerned and careful, wanting to be honest and kind at once, which fits his line that it was not fine but it is not the end.

qa.q: What did Rafiq offer that gave Irawati a next step?
qa.a: Rafiq offered to go through only the mistake at lunch the next day with his board. That made the problem small and workable.

qa.q: Why might Irawati have thanked Rafiq for not saying it was fine?
qa.a: Irawati may have felt that empty reassurance would ignore her real disappointment. Rafiq's honesty let her feel heard.

grounding: A friend responds to despair by staying, listening and pointing to a small next step, not by insisting everything will be fine.

"You didn't come to lunch," Devika said, finding Lokesh on the back stairs.
"Didn't get into the state orchestra." His voice was flat. "Two years of practice. For nothing."
Devika sat down beside him. She didn't say anything for a bit.
"Go on, say it'll be fine," he muttered.
"I wasn't going to. It's awful. You practised every day."
"Every. Single. Day."
They sat. A bell rang somewhere.
"Did they say anything about why?" she asked.
"The judge said my bowing was stiff in the fast part."
"Hm. Mr. Pinto helped Karan with bowing last year. Want to go ask him at break? I'll come."
Lokesh wiped his nose with his sleeve. "You'll come?"
"I'll come."
He picked up his violin case. "Okay. Break."

qa.a: The judge said his bowing was stiff in the fast part.

qa.q: Why did Devika stay quiet at first instead of cheering Lokesh up?

qa.q: What did Devika do that passed on hope?
qa.a: She stayed, admitted it was awful instead of promising it would be fine, and offered to go with him to Mr. Pinto at break.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Devika said 'I'll come'?
qa.a: He probably felt less alone and a bit hopeful, since someone was staying beside him for the next step.

Last autumn, Lalremsiami tore a ligament two weeks before the state football trials. She had trained for three years. When I found her in the physio room at school, she wasn't crying. She was just staring at the wall, which was worse.
I wanted to say, "You'll be back stronger," because everyone was saying that. I could see it made her flinch.
So I just sat down. I stayed there through the whole of the next period, which got me a warning. She talked a little about her dad, who'd driven her to every practice. Then she was quiet.
Before I left I asked, "Can I bring my laptop tomorrow? We can watch the trials together, and you can tell me who you'd pick." She almost smiled. "Okay."
I'm Amandeep. We watched every match. She tried out again the next year.

qa.q: When did Lalremsiami tear a ligament?
qa.a: Two weeks before the state football trials.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling on hearing everyone say 'You'll be back stronger'?
qa.a: Amandeep felt uneasy and worried, seeing how the promise made Lalremsiami flinch, and wanted to offer something truer.

qa.q: What small step did Amandeep offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: Watching the trials together tomorrow gave Lalremsiami company and a small reason to stay connected to football, instead of a promise.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when Amandeep suggested watching the trials together?
qa.a: She probably felt a flicker of hope and company, since she almost smiled.

grounding: Shows a teenager answering a friend's despair with presence and a small next step rather than promises.

passage:
Athletics coach's note, Saturday, district meet.
Pallavi (15) fell in the 800 m final, 50 metres from the line. She finished last and walked straight off the track to sit behind the stands. I was about to go to her when I saw Vijay, from her training group, get there first.
He didn't say "Never mind" or "Next time for sure." He sat beside her and listened while she said she was quitting. He said, "That was a horrible fall." After a long time he asked, "Want to walk the track with me tomorrow morning, before anyone's here? Just walk it."
She nodded. I gave them both ten minutes, then joined them, checked her knee, and phoned her mother to tell her what happened. I'll be at the track at seven tomorrow.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi fall in the 800 m final?
qa.a: 50 metres from the line.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling behind the stands?
qa.a: She felt crushed and hopeless, saying she was quitting.

qa.q: What did the coach do next that supported both young people?
qa.a: The coach gave them ten minutes, then joined them, checked Pallavi's knee, phoned her mother and planned to be at the track at seven.

qa.q: How might Vijay have seen Pallavi's fall?
qa.a: He seemed to understand how painful it was, calling it a horrible fall, and wanted to stay with her rather than cheer her up quickly.

grounding: Shows a teenager answering a friend's despair by staying, listening and offering a small step, passing on hope through presence.

Thursday
Sonali's diary. Parveen didn't come to lunch, so I found her behind the library, knees up, not crying, just staring. Her abbu's shop is closing and they're moving to her uncle's town in June. "Everything's finished," she said. "My friends, school, all of it." I almost said "It'll be fine!" but it won't be, not all of it, and she'd know I was lying. So I just sat. I didn't talk. After a long time she told me about the new school, and that her ammi cries in the kitchen at night. I asked what one thing would make June less scary. She said, "Knowing when I'd see you." So we made a plan: first holidays, she visits. I walked her home, and her ammi came to the gate and hugged her. Parveen said she'd talk to her ammi properly tonight.

qa.q: Where did Sonali find Parveen?
qa.a: Behind the library, sitting with her knees up.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stop before saying "It'll be fine!"?
qa.a: Sonali felt it would be dishonest, since not all of it would be fine, and was worried Parveen would know it was a lie.

qa.q: Which part of Sonali's response helped most?
qa.a: Sitting quietly and then asking about one thing that would make June less scary, which led to a real plan instead of empty cheer.

qa.q: What was it like for Parveen to have Sonali just sit with her?
qa.a: She probably felt less alone and safe enough to talk about the new school and her ammi crying at night.

grounding: Shows a friend answering another's despair by staying, listening and finding one small next step instead of promising everything will be fine.
